en.title: DCU's Clayface Movie Finds Its Best Version in Unexpected Place
en.summary: While the upcoming DCU movie taps into **Batman: The Animated Series** for inspiration, a surprising earlier show offered a more compelling take on the shapeshifting villain. Get ready to dive into the darker, more tragic arcs that define the true potential of Clayface.
en.body:
The upcoming DCU movie **Clayface**, slated for an October 23, 2026 release, has confirmed its inspiration lies heavily in the beloved **Batman: The Animated Series** two-part episode, “Feat of Clay.” This classic tale introduced audiences to the tragic origins of Matt Hagen, a struggling actor desperate to regain his looks and career through a mysterious face-changing serum. It’s a foundational story, layering detective work with villainous pathos, and it's understandable why new DC Studios heads **James Gunn** and **Peter Safran** would look to it for a modern adaptation, especially given director **Mike Flanagan**'s initial script development.

However, while “Feat of Clay” is undoubtedly a landmark episode, it's not the *only* animated series to offer a truly compelling Clayface. Years before the DCU was even a concept, **The Batman**, which premiered in 2004, delivered a surprisingly dark and character-driven take on the villain in its season one finale. The two-part episode, “The Rubberface of Comedy/The Clayface of Tragedy,” reimagined Clayface not as a born villain, but as a victim of circumstance and horrific transformation. In this iteration, Detective Ethan Bennet is captured by the Joker, subjected to a terrifying psychological ordeal, and injected with a substance that fundamentally alters his physical form and mental state. This story arc emphasizes the tragedy and horror of losing control over one’s own body and identity, a potent thematic core that resonates deeply.

## A More Tragic Transformation

The brilliance of **The Batman**'s Clayface lies in its commitment to the character’s descent. Unlike the more straightforwardly tragic Matt Hagen of **Batman: The Animated Series**, Detective Bennet's transformation is a direct result of a villain's cruel machinations. This external catalyst amplifies the horror, making his plight feel less like a consequence of personal ambition and more like a brutal violation. The showrunners leaned into the grotesque nature of his powers, presenting a Clayface that was as pitiable as he was monstrous. This approach provided a richer narrative for fans who appreciate the psychological depth and darker undercurrents that can elevate superhero storytelling beyond simple good versus evil.

## What This Means for the DCU

As the DCU gears up to introduce its own version of Clayface, the success of **The Batman**’s arc offers a valuable blueprint. While the inspiration from **Batman: The Animated Series** is clear, the darker, more psychologically tormenting path taken by **The Batman** might hold the key to creating a truly memorable villain for a new generation. Fans have long debated which iteration best captures the essence of the character, and the upcoming film has an opportunity to synthesize these elements. The shift from **Mike Flanagan**'s initial script to a new one by writer **Amini** indicates that the DCU is still refining its vision, and drawing from the most impactful interpretations across animation history will be crucial for **Clayface**'s success.

## What's Next

The **Clayface** movie is scheduled for release on October 23, 2026. Details regarding the full cast and director are still emerging, but the confirmed inspiration from classic animated stories sets a high bar for narrative ambition.

content_raw: Since Clayface began production, one key influence has lingered over the movie. Mike Flanagan , who penned the screenplay, named the Batman: The Animated Series two-part episode “Feat of Clay” as a major inspiration . Flanagan chose well, as “Feat of Clay” has all the hallmarks of a great Batman story. It features the Dark Knight using his detective skills to solve the mystery of why someone who looks like Bruce Wayne is committing crimes. It layers tragedy into its villain’s life, as Matt Hagen seeks more face-changing serum to regain his movie-star looks. And it all borders on the horrific because of Clayface’s shape-changing abilities. But while “Feat of Clay” is a remarkable…feat, there’s a Batman show out there with a more compelling version of Clayface: The Batman . The Batman debuted in 2004 on the now-defunct Kids WB channel and faced an uphill battle from its first episode. The animated series arrived at the tail end of Justice League Unlimited ’s run, inviting unfair comparisons. Fans also bristled at the idea of a younger Bruce Wayne who ate nachos and went to basketball games, though that arguably fit the persona of an early-2000s playboy. Driven mad, Bennett tries to kill his former commanding officer, Commissioner Rojas, but Batman stops him. “The Rubberface of Comedy” and “The Clayface of Tragedy” hit hard because they fit the standard Batman trope of Bruce Wayne’s friend becoming a supervillain (see also: Tommy Elliot a.k.a. Hush and Talia al Ghul). Before these episodes, Bennett and Bruce were best friends; Bennett even stood up for Batman’s vigilante activities, opposing his partner, Ellen Yin. Seeing him become Clayface is truly tragic: Bruce Wayne lost a friend, and Batman gained an enemy. Future episodes only further heightened that tragedy, as Bennett struggled to maintain his grasp on sanity but fell to his homicidal tendencies. What makes The Batman ’s take on Clayface stand out is that it mirrors another iconic foe in Two-Face. Like Ethan Bennett, Harvey Dent was an ally of Batman’s who suffered an event that left him physically and mentally scarred. Since Two-Face never showed up in The Batman , Clayface took his place as Batman’s most tragic foe.
